q: Your Node app runs in a container and calls console.log. Where should the log lines go?
options: Into a file named app.log inside the container
To stdout and stderr, so Docker can keep them and docker logs can read them
Into the database, one row per line
Nowhere, containers do not keep logs
why: The app only prints. Docker catches stdout and stderr and keeps them in a file on the host. A file inside the container is lost when the container is removed.

q: A container runs for a year with Docker's default log settings (json-file). What stops its log file from growing?
options: Docker rotates the file at 10 MB by default
Linux deletes the oldest lines by itself
Nothing, because max-size is unlimited by default
The container restarts every week
why: The Docker docs say max-size defaults to -1 (unlimited). In my test the container with defaults kept all 2003 lines (195,236 bytes), and the one with max-size 10k and max-file 3 kept 133 lines (13,052 bytes).

q: Three requests run at the same time, so their log lines are mixed. Which field lets you pull out the lines of one customer's request?
options: The log level
The time
The request id
The message text
why: The level says how bad a line is. The request id says whose line it is. Three requests ran at the same moment, so the time cannot tell them apart.

q: Errors per minute at 23:14, 23:15 and 23:16 are 12, 14 and 4. The rule is: 5 or more errors, 2 minutes in a row. When does the alert fire?
options: At 23:14, the first bad minute
At 23:15, the minute that completes 2 bad minutes in a row
At 23:16, after all three minutes
It never fires
why: 23:14 is the first bad minute, and one is not enough. 23:15 is bad too and touches it, so the run is complete. 23:16 has only 4 errors and does not matter any more.

q: A container with a failing HEALTHCHECK turns unhealthy. It runs with plain Docker and --restart=always. What does Docker do?
options: It restarts the container at once
It stops and removes the container
Nothing but change the state to unhealthy, so something else must act
It sends an email
why: In my test the state became unhealthy after 3 failed checks, and RestartCount stayed 0 with the policy set to always. Docker Swarm and Kubernetes can act on the state. Plain Docker does not.

q: Docker says your container is healthy, but users cannot open the site. What is the best extra check?
options: A check from outside, like a visitor, that asks the public address
A second health check inside the same container
A higher log level
Nothing, the health check is enough
why: A check inside sees only the container. A broken proxy, DNS or certificate stays invisible from inside. A check from another machine sees what users see.
